description.p: Soulless is a launcher for the COSMIC desktop, built by one stubborn veteran who decided everything on a computer should be findable from a single search box — apps, files, folders, CLI tools, Steam games, Flatpaks, Snaps, the whole lot. No hunting through menus. No five different places to look. One box, type, go.

It also does a few things most launchers don't bother with. The search learns as you go — the apps and tools you actually open float to the top, ranked by how often and how recently you reach for them, so the stuff you use is always one keystroke away. It keeps an eye on your Downloads folder too: drop a file in and Soulless works out where it belongs — pictures to Pictures, videos to Videos, that invoice to Finance — tells you why, and files it away with one click. It only ever suggests; nothing moves without your say-so.

And it makes CLI tools actually useful by launching their man pages — search a command, hit it, and read the docs instead of squinting at a bare name. Stash your sensitive files and apps behind an encrypted vault so they vanish from every menu on the system. Sort your tools into custom drawers that make sense to you. And keep an eye on your hardware with live network, CPU, GPU, RAM, and per-monitor FPS readouts while you work.

ul.li: Search that learns — the more you use something, the higher it ranks, by frequency and recency
Smart download sorting — reads each new file, suggests where it belongs and why, files it with one click, and never moves anything without permission
Universal search — apps, files, CLI tools, Steam, Flatpak, and Snap, all at once
CLI tools that launch their man pages, so a command is actually useful and not just a name
Custom drawers to organize your tools the way your brain works, not the way a menu thinks it should
Encrypted vault that pulls sensitive files and apps off every system menu
Live hardware monitors — network, CPU, GPU, RAM, per-monitor FPS
Your own backgrounds from ~/.config/soulless/backgrounds/
Disk-cached index so it opens the instant you hit the key
Full keyboard navigation — Tab, S, V, arrows, no mouse required
Super+Space from anywhere
wgpu-accelerated rendering because it's 2026

description.p: Keyboard shortcut works from the first keypress: the launcher daemon previously started only on the first applet click, so a shortcut pressed before any click found nothing to talk to -- and its own process became a mute daemon that wedged the applet button until logout. The applet now starts the daemon the moment the panel loads, and the stray instance problem is gone.

Residency guard for the sandbox: launching Soulless any way other than the panel applet (the store's Open button, a terminal run, the shortcut) lands on a Wayland socket that cannot create the launcher's window. Such launches now step aside with a logged explanation instead of silently taking over and breaking the applet button.

Login race fixed: at login, two launcher daemons could race for the D-Bus name. The loser survived invisibly, holding a full-screen surface that ate every desktop click until logout. A kernel file lock now referees the race — one daemon wins, the loser delivers its activation and exits.

Panel-birth guard: if the launcher's main app id ends up in the panel's applet list, cosmic-panel execs a headless launcher at every panel start — an impostor that squatted the D-Bus name and ate clicks. The launcher now refuses residency when born as a panel child without the applet's blessing, and logs the cure.

Sandbox placement fixed: the Flatpak redirects XDG_CONFIG_HOME and renames the applet's desktop id, so the launcher could never find the panel config — store installs always opened dead center. The launcher now reads the host config and matches both applet identities; the window opens at the applet's corner, native and Flatpak alike.

Window placement is now exact at every panel size: instead of estimating the panel's thickness from its config, the launcher asks the compositor to carve the panel and dock out of its surface -- placement inherits their true rendered size, XS through XL, padding included.

Version 2.0. A hundred and twenty-three commits since 1.0 — the Flatpak fought back and lost, the FPS widget learned to count every screen honestly, and the prototype era is over. Everything below is in the git log; nothing here is aspirational.

ul.li: Flatpak works for real — the window opens in-sandbox via the compositor's privileged-socket handoff, the indexer reads the host system under /run/host, and launches route through the host, so store users get the same launcher as source builds

Per-monitor FPS widget — a live census of every connected display with connector name, configured Hz, and true per-screen fps from filtered compositor ticks; plug a monitor in and its cell appears, pull the cable and it leaves

Search overhaul — virtualized uncapped results, smart queries answer first ("game" means games, "new" means recently installed), folders split from files, and the per-keystroke allocation storm is dead
Right-click uninstall for Steam, Flatpak, and AppImage entries
A real CLI — the soulless wrapper, a man page, --help and --version, and soulless-launcher toggle routed to the warm daemon
Indexes stay fresh — re-index on activation, caches watch the Steam and AppImage dirs, no more ghost tiles or invisible new installs
Runtime theming — theme.ron with hex colors and partial overrides, every bare color swept to tokens, zero corner radii enforced launcher-wide, widget heights split short and tall
Honest hardware stats — a shared NVML handle with a sysfs fallback for non-NVIDIA boxes, a dash instead of a fake 0%, ping moved off the UI executor
Organizer doctrine — types only: extensions are facts, filenames are claims; Skip is remembered, and pruned when the file disappears
Vault — hide apps from any source by name identity; the twin-door identity leak is closed
Widget pages — dot-selected pages with a scratch terminal box
Placement — the launcher follows its applet, click-away dismisses, blur scoped to the launcher region

description.p: Version 1.0. Three days of coffee, cigarettes, and questionable decisions to drag this across the finish line. It builds, it runs, and everything in the feature list actually works. Whether it's any good is for you to decide — but it does what it says.
